query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent, slow-growing protective oxide layer forms and persists above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than cracking or spalling? Earlier work investigated CrFeCoNiX and CrMoTiAlY (Y = Ta, Nb, or W) alloy systems and reported that some compositions developed unstable surface oxides prone to cracking and spallation, while the underlying physical causes remain unresolved. Given the requirement for an environmentally stable, chemically inert barrier and prolonged structural integrity, specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted observations, the relevant composition, material-state, exposure, and service boundaries, the prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and long-term persistence of a protective oxide scale above 900 °C is driven by the preferential oxidation of the X element, which controls the diffusion kinetics and lattice coherence at the oxide/alloy interface. In particular, when X = Al, the alloy favors formation of a coherent, low-defect Al2O3 scale that grows slowly and adheres strongly to the substrate, while when X = Si or Mn the resulting oxides exhibit higher defect densities and larger thermal mismatch, promoting cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state
generation.intervention: Expose alloy samples to a controlled oxidative/corrosive atmosphere at temperatures exceeding 900 °C
generation.conditions: Temperature above 900 °C, controlled oxygen partial pressure (or corrosive environment), and sufficient exposure duration (e.g., 100–300 hours) to monitor the evolution of the oxide scale under service-like conditions
generation.structural_mediator: The preferential oxidation of element X leads to formation of an oxide layer whose coherence is mediated by its crystallographic match and low thermal expansion mismatch with the underlying alloy, thus strongly influencing diffusion paths for both oxygen and cations
generation.mechanism: When X = Al, the thermodynamic stability and low oxygen diffusivity of Al2O3 form a continuous, slow-growing, and coherent oxide layer that minimizes further oxidation by reducing ionic transport. In contrast, when X = Si or Mn, the oxides formed are less structurally compatible with the alloy substrate, leading to a higher density of defects and mismatch-induced stresses that promote cracking or spallation of the oxide scale.
generation.predicted_outcome: Al-containing alloys will develop a thin, slowly growing, and adherent oxide layer with minimal cracking, while Si- or Mn-containing alloys will form oxide scales that, despite possibly growing faster, exhibit significant cracking or spallation under identical high-temperature exposure conditions.
generation.baseline: Alloys where the role of element X does not yield a coherent oxide (or a control alloy with a composition known to form non-protective oxide scales) will show rapidly growing, non-uniform, and spalled oxide layers under the same exposure conditions.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in single- or multiphase solid-solution states, exposed to oxidative/corrosive atmospheres at temperatures >900 °C over extended durations (100–300 hours). It is bounded by the specific alloy compositions and environmental conditions that affect oxidation kinetics and lattice matching phenomena.
generation.uncertainty: Uncertainty remains regarding the quantitative differences in cation diffusivity and lattice mismatch for each X element and whether these differences alone can account for the observed oxide scale stability, pending further experimental data on diffusion parameters and interfacial stresses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare alloy samples of CrFeCoNiX with X = Si, Mn, and Al. Expose all samples simultaneously to a controlled oxidative (or corrosive) environment at temperatures above 900 °C for 100–300 hours. Characterize the oxide layers periodically using in-situ high-temperature microscopy, X-ray diffraction, and electron microscopy to assess oxide thickness, phase, and interfacial integrity.
measurements: Oxide layer thickness as a function of time
Crack density and incidence of spallation via microscopy
Phase identification and microstructural analysis (e.g., XRD/EBSD) to evaluate oxide crystallinity/coherence
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloys do not exhibit a significantly more coherent, slow-growing, and adherent oxide layer compared to the Si- or Mn-containing alloys under identical test conditions, then the hypothesis that preferential oxidation of element X governs oxide stability is falsified.
